claim: Euarthropods are an extremely diverse phylum in the modern, and have been since their origination in the early Palaeozoic.
source: Euarthropods are an extremely diverse phylum in the modern, and have been since their origination in the early Palaeozoic.
evidence: This is a general statement about euarthropod diversity supported by established scientific knowledge about the fossil record and modern biodiversity.

claim: Euarthropods grow through moulting the exoskeleton (ecdysis) facilitated by breaking along lines of weakness (sutures).
source: They grow through moulting the exoskeleton (ecdysis) facilitated by breaking along lines of weakness (sutures).
evidence: This is established knowledge about arthropod biology and growth mechanisms.

claim: Artiopodans, a group that includes trilobites and their non-biomineralizing relatives, dominated arthropod diversity in benthic communities during the Palaeozoic.
source: Artiopodans, a group that includes trilobites and their non-biomineralizing relatives, dominated arthropod diversity in benthic communities during the Palaeozoic.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Daley et al., 2018 in the Introduction section.

claim: Most trilobites moult by breaking the exoskeleton along cephalic sutures.
source: Most trilobites – a hyperdiverse group of tens of thousands of species - moult by breaking the exoskeleton along cephalic sutures, a strategy that has contributed to their high diversity during the Palaeozoic.
evidence: This is established knowledge about trilobite biology supported by extensive literature on trilobite morphology and ecdysis.

claim: The moulting strategy of breaking the exoskeleton along cephalic sutures has contributed to trilobite high diversity during the Palaeozoic.
source: Most trilobites – a hyperdiverse group of tens of thousands of species - moult by breaking the exoskeleton along cephalic sutures, a strategy that has contributed to their high diversity during the Palaeozoic.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of cephalic sutures in trilobite evolution.

claim: Similar sutures to those in trilobites have been described in early diverging non-trilobite artiopodans.
source: However, the recent description of similar sutures in early diverging non-trilobite artiopodans means that it is unclear whether these sutures evolved deep within Artiopoda, or convergently appeared multiple times within the group.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature on artiopodan morphology.

claim: Artiopoda is united by a morphology consisting of a headshield covering a pair of uniramous antennae and at least three pairs of biramous limbs, followed by a dorsoventrally flattened body with a series of biramous appendages.
source: This group, which includes trilobites and their non-biomineralizing relatives, are united by a morphology consisting of a headshield covering a pair of uniramous antennae and at least three pairs of biramous limbs, followed by a dorsoventrally flattened body with a series of biramous appendages (Stein and Selden, 2012; Giribet and Edgecombe, 2019).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by citations to Stein and Selden, 2012 and Giribet and Edgecombe, 2019.

claim: The origins of key morphological features facilitating the diversity of trilobites can be found in their non-biomineralizing artiopodan relatives.
source: The origins of key morphological features facilitating the diversity of trilobites can be found in their non-biomineralizing artiopodan relatives (e.g. Du et al., 2019; Schmidt et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Du et al., 2019 and Schmidt et al., 2022.

claim: The presence, shape, and character of sutures in the trilobite cephalon have been central to classification schemes of the group for nearly 200 years.
source: The presence, shape, and character of sutures in the trilobite cephalon have been central to classification schemes of the group for nearly 200 years (e.g. Emmrich, 1839; Salter, 1864; Beecher, 1897a; Beecher, 1897b; Stubblefield, 1936; Rasetti, 1945; Whittington et al., 1997)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple historical citations spanning from 1839 to 1997.

claim: The similarity in the cranidial outlines of Cambrian suture-bearing groups supported a single origin or strong evolutionary constraint on its origins.
source: while the similarity in the cranidial outlines of Cambrian suture-bearing groups supported a single origin or strong evolutionary constraint on its origins (Foote, 1991; Hughes, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Foote, 1991 and Hughes, 2007.

claim: Sutures in trilobites provided lines of weakness along which the cephalon split during moulting, creating an anterior ecdysial gape through which the animal exited the old exoskeleton.
source: These sutures provided lines of weakness along which the cephalon split during moulting, creating an anterior ecdysial gape through which the animal exited the old exoskeleton (e.g. Henningsmoen, 1975; Whittington, 1990; Daley and Drage, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Henningsmoen, 1975; Whittington, 1990; and Daley and Drage, 2016.

claim: Sutures in trilobites may have served additional purposes beyond ecdysis, including feeding and burrowing behaviours.
source: Sutures may have served additional purposes (Stubblefield, 1936) and were under additional functional demands, including feeding (Fortey and Owens, 1999) and burrowing behaviours (Esteve et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stubblefield, 1936; Fortey and Owens, 1999; and Esteve et al., 2021.

claim: For the earliest diverging trilobites, olenellines, circumocular sutures facilitated shedding of the cornea during ecdysis.
source: For the earliest diverging trilobites, olenellines (Palmer and Repina, 1993; Lieberman, 2002) which a have been recovered as a paraphyletic grade rather than a monophyletic group (e.g. Paterson et al., 2019) circumocular sutures facilitated shedding of the cornea during ecdysis (e.g. Ramsköld and Edgecombe, 1991)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ramsköld and Edgecombe, 1991.

claim: Olenellines have been recovered as a paraphyletic grade rather than a monophyletic group.
source: For the earliest diverging trilobites, olenellines (Palmer and Repina, 1993; Lieberman, 2002) which a have been recovered as a paraphyletic grade rather than a monophyletic group (e.g. Paterson et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Paterson et al., 2019.

claim: In olenellines, a marginal suture facilitated anterior egression through separation of the lateral cephalic doublure from the dorsal cephalon.
source: while a marginal suture (Figure 1e) facilitated anterior egression through separation of the lateral cephalic doublure from the dorsal cephalon (e.g. Stubblefield, 1936; Henningsmoen, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stubblefield, 1936 and Henningsmoen, 1975, and reference to Figure 1e.

claim: In later diverging trilobites, the circumocular and marginal sutures combined into a single system.
source: In later diverging trilobites the circumocular and marginal sutures combined into a single system (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1d and established knowledge about trilobite morphology.

claim: In later diverging trilobites, the cornea is fused to the free cheek.
source: Here, the cornea is fused to the free cheek (e.g. Stubblefield, 1936; Ramsköld and Edgecombe, 1991)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stubblefield, 1936 and Ramsköld and Edgecombe, 1991.

claim: The origin of fused dorsal ecdysial sutures (facial sutures) has traditionally been considered to fall within Trilobita.
source: The origin of these fused dorsal ecdysial sutures – facial sutures – has traditionally been considered to fall within Trilobita (e.g. Fortey and Whittington, 1989; Edgecombe and Ramsköld, 1999; Lieberman, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fortey and Whittington, 1989; Edgecombe and Ramsköld, 1999; and Lieberman, 2002.

claim: The presence of dorsal ecdysial sutures in earlier diverging artiopodans raised questions about the homology and origins within Artiopoda.
source: However, the presence of dorsal ecdysial sutures in earlier diverging artiopodans – the Protosutura (Du et al., 2019) and eye slits in Petalopleura (Chen et al., 2019) raised questions about the homology and origins within Artiopoda (e.g. Hou et al., 2017b; Du et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Du et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019; and Hou et al., 2017b.

claim: An alternative hypothesis proposes that dorsal cephalic sutures had a deep root within Artiopoda and were subsequently lost in some groups including multiple times within Trilobita.
source: An alternative hypothesis for the origins of the dorsal cephalic sutures emerged: that these had a deep root within Artiopoda and were subsequently lost in some groups including multiple times within Trilobita (Hou et al., 2017b; Du et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hou et al., 2017b and Du et al., 2019.

claim: Support for the deep root hypothesis comes from the variability of facial sutures in trilobites, and the recognition that convergence and loss of features is common when they have a function or allow adaptation to a particular niche.
source: Support for the deep root hypothesis comes from the variability of facial sutures in trilobites, and the recognition that convergence and loss of features is common when they have a function or allow adapation to a particular niche (e.g. Moore and Willmer, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moore and Willmer, 1997 and inference about evolutionary patterns.

claim: Dalmanitinid facial sutures fuse during ontogeny.
source: Further evidence for the variability of suture morphology comes from ontogenetic studies, such as the fusion of dalmanitinid facial sutures during ontogeny (Drage et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Drage et al., 2018.

claim: The facial suture has been lost in some trilobites such as 'Cedaria' woosteri.
source: and the loss of this feature in other trilobites such as 'Cedaria' woosteri (Hughes et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hughes et al., 1997.

claim: Acanthomeridion serratum has a subtriangular head shield with deep lateral notches that accommodate stalked elliptical eyes.
source: Subtriangular head shield with deep lateral notches that accommodate stalked elliptical eyes, rounded genal angles of the head shield, an axe-like hypostome, and paired teardrop-shaped plates on either side of the hypostome.
evidence: This is a morphological description based on direct observation of specimens.

claim: Acanthomeridion serratum has an axe-like hypostome.
source: Subtriangular head shield with deep lateral notches that accommodate stalked elliptical eyes, rounded genal angles of the head shield, an axe-like hypostome, and paired teardrop-shaped plates on either side of the hypostome.
evidence: This is a morphological description based on direct observation of specimens.

claim: Acanthomeridion serratum has paired teardrop-shaped plates on either side of the hypostome.
source: Subtriangular head shield with deep lateral notches that accommodate stalked elliptical eyes, rounded genal angles of the head shield, an axe-like hypostome, and paired teardrop-shaped plates on either side of the hypostome.
evidence: This is a morphological description based on direct observation of specimens.

claim: Acanthomeridion serratum has long multi-segmented antennae consisting of over 40 articles.
source: Head bears large eyes and long multi-segmented antennae consisting of over 40 articles anterior to three pairs of small cephalic limbs.
evidence: This is a morphological description based on direct observation of specimens.

claim: Acanthomeridion serratum has three pairs of small cephalic limbs.
source: Head bears large eyes and long multi-segmented antennae consisting of over 40 articles anterior to three pairs of small cephalic limbs.
evidence: This is a morphological description based on direct observation of specimens.

claim: The trunk of Acanthomeridion serratum is composed of 11 tergites bearing expanded tergopleurae with well-developed distal spines.
source: The trunk is composed of 11 tergites bearing expanded tergopleurae with well-developed distal spines, and a terminal spine.
evidence: This is a morphological description based on direct observation of specimens.

claim: The ninth tergite of Acanthomeridion serratum bears a pleural spine more elongated than others.
source: The ninth tergite bears a pleural spine more elongated than others, the eleventh tergite is reduced and expanded into a leaf-like outline.
evidence: This is a morphological description based on direct observation of specimens.

claim: The eleventh tergite of Acanthomeridion serratum is reduced and expanded into a leaf-like outline.
source: The ninth tergite bears a pleural spine more elongated than others, the eleventh tergite is reduced and expanded into a leaf-like outline.
evidence: This is a morphological description based on direct observation of specimens.

claim: Each tergite of Acanthomeridion serratum bears a pair of biramous limbs with long and dense spines on the endopodites, and slender stick-like exopodites with long and dense bristles.
source: Each tergite bears a pair of biramous limbs with long and dense spines on the endopodites, and slender stick-like exopodites with long and dense bristles.
evidence: This is a morphological description based on direct observation of specimens.

claim: Acanthomeridion anacanthus is a junior subjective synonym of Acanthomeridion serratum.
source: Acanthomeridion anacanthus Hou et al., 2017b is here proposed to be a junior subjective synonym of Acanthomeridion serratum Hou et al., 1989
evidence: This is a taxonomic conclusion based on morphological analysis and bivariate regression analysis of specimens.

claim: Specimens of Acanthomeridion serratum measure from 20 to 75 mm along the sagittal axis.
source: Specimens measure from 20 to 75 mm along the sagittal axis (Figure 3a and c; Figure 4; Figure 5a; Figure 6; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is a measurement based on direct observation of specimens shown in figures.

claim: The head shield of Acanthomeridion serratum becomes wider relative to its length during ontogeny.
source: The head shield becomes wider relative to its length during ontogeny (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of specimens of different sizes shown in Figure 6.

claim: The ventral plates of Acanthomeridion serratum have a teardrop outline and occupy the entire length of the cephalon.
source: Ventral plates have a teardrop outline, occupy the entire length of the cephalon and terminate in a posterior spine (maximum length 3.4 mm; Figure 3—figure supplement 2b) that projects into the thorax as far as the anteriormost tergite (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a morphological description based on direct observation of specimens shown in figures.

claim: The ventral plates of Acanthomeridion serratum terminate in a posterior spine with maximum length 3.4 mm.
source: Ventral plates have a teardrop outline, occupy the entire length of the cephalon and terminate in a posterior spine (maximum length 3.4 mm; Figure 3—figure supplement 2b) that projects into the thorax as far as the anteriormost tergite (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a measurement based on direct observation of specimens.

claim: Four pairs of appendages are present in the head of Acanthomeridion serratum.
source: Four pairs of appendages are present in the head (Figure 3f–j; Figure 3—figure supplement 5a).
evidence: This is a morphological observation based on specimens shown in figures.

claim: The antennae of Acanthomeridion serratum have at least 43 articles.
source: A pair of antennae with at least 43 articles (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a, f; Figure 3—figure supplement 4; Figure 5a and b) sits anterior to three pairs of small cephalic limbs (Figure 3f–j).
evidence: This is a count based on direct observation of specimens shown in figures.

claim: Articles of the antennae of Acanthomeridion serratum decrease in length and width distally.
source: Articles of the antennae decrease in length and width distally.
evidence: This is a morphological observation based on specimens.

claim: The preserved part of the antennae of Acanthomeridion serratum is slightly shorter than the trunk.
source: The preserved part of the antennae is slightly shorter than the trunk (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a comparative observation based on specimens shown in Figure 5.

claim: The protopodite of the cephalic limbs of Acanthomeridion serratum are subtriangular in outline.
source: The protopodite of the cephalic limbs are subtriangular in outline.
evidence: This is a morphological description based on direct observation of specimens.

claim: Tergites 8–11 of Acanthomeridion serratum curve towards the posterior and reduce in width progressively.
source: Tergites 8–11 curve towards the posterior, and reduce in width progressively, so that T11 is approximately 25% the width of T8 and 33% the width of T9 (Figure 3a and c; Figure 4, Figure 5a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a morphological observation with measurements based on specimens shown in figures.

claim: T11 of Acanthomeridion serratum is approximately 25% the width of T8 and 33% the width of T9.
source: Tergites 8–11 curve towards the posterior, and reduce in width progressively, so that T11 is approximately 25% the width of T8 and 33% the width of T9 (Figure 3a and c; Figure 4, Figure 5a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a measurement based on direct observation of specimens shown in figures.

claim: Each tergite of Acanthomeridion serratum has small spines on its lateral and posterior margins.
source: Each tergite has small spines on its lateral and posterior margins (Figure 4a; Figure 7; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2i, k; Figure 3—figure supplement 3a, j; Figure 3—figure supplements 5b, e, f and 6a–f).
evidence: This is a morphological observation based on specimens shown in multiple figures.

claim: The shape of tergites and the convexity of the trunk of Acanthomeridion serratum changes through ontogeny.
source: The shape of tergites and the convexity of the trunk changes through ontogeny (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of specimens of different sizes shown in Figure 7.

claim: In smaller specimens of Acanthomeridion serratum, the trunk appears slender from a dorsal view as the body displays a high convexity.
source: In the smaller specimens, the trunk appears slender from a dorsal view as the body displays a high convexity (Figure 6t).
evidence: This is an observation based on specimens shown in Figure 6t.

claim: In larger specimens of Acanthomeridion serratum, the trunk is less convex than for the smaller specimens.
source: In larger specimens, the trunk is less convex than for the smaller specimens (Figure 6s)
evidence: This is an observation based on specimens shown in Figure 6s.

claim: A linear relationship between trunk axial length and width is obtained for Acanthomeridion serratum.
source: A linear relationship between trunk axial length and width is obtained (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a statistical result based on measurements shown in Figure 7.

claim: The protopodite of trunk appendages of Acanthomeridion serratum is sub-triangular with a broad attachment to the body wall and short robust gnathobasal spines along the medial margin.
source: The protopodite is sub-triangular with a broad attachment to the body wall and short robust gnathobasal spines along the medial margin (Figure 3h–j; Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–f, i).
evidence: This is a morphological description based on specimens shown in figures.

claim: The ventral margin of the protopodite of Acanthomeridion serratum has endites longer than the gnathobasal spines.
source: The ventral margin of the protopodite has endites longer than the gnathobasal spines.
evidence: This is a morphological observation based on specimens.

claim: Exopodites of Acanthomeridion serratum are slender, stick-like, and long (8.3 mm, ca. 3 x protopodite length), bearing two rows of lamellae.
source: Exopodites are slender, stick-like, and long (8.3 mm, ca. 3 x protopodite length), bearing two rows of lamellae (Figure 3h, i and k; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a morphological description with measurements based on specimens shown in figures.

claim: Exopodites of Acanthomeridion serratum are shorter than the width of corresponding tergites.
source: Exopodites are shorter than the width of corresponding tergites (Figure 3h; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a comparative observation based on specimens shown in figures.

claim: There is no evidence that the exopodite of Acanthomeridion serratum is divided into lobes or has articulations.
source: There is no evidence that the exopodite is divided into lobes or has articulations.
evidence: This is an observation based on examination of specimens.

claim: Endopodites of Acanthomeridion serratum are composed of seven trapezoidal podomeres.
source: Endopodites are composed of seven trapezoidal podomeres.
evidence: This is a morphological observation based on specimens.

claim: Podomeres 1–6 of the endopodites of Acanthomeridion serratum bear spiniferous endites arranged in rows.
source: Podomeres 1–6 bear spiniferous endites arranged in rows, six on pd1, 2, 4 on pd3, 4, and 3 on pd5, 6.
evidence: This is a morphological observation with counts based on specimens.

claim: Podomere seven of the endopodites of Acanthomeridion serratum displays a terminal claw of three elongated spines.
source: Podomere seven displays a terminal claw of three elongated spines (Figure 3h and k; Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a morphological observation based on specimens shown in figures.

claim: One specimen of Acanthomeridion serratum shows evidence of paired midgut diverticulae.
source: One specimen shows evidence of paired midgut diverticulae (Figure 3—figure supplement 4a, f).
evidence: This is an observation based on a specimen shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4a, f.

claim: The body of Acanthomeridion serratum terminates in a long, slender spine, dorsal to a paired paddle-like structure.
source: The body terminates in a long, slender spine, dorsal to a paired paddle-like structure (Figure 5a and e; Figure 3—figure supplement 5b, g; Figure 3—figure supplement 6g, i).
evidence: This is a morphological observation based on specimens shown in figures.

claim: The ventral plates of Acanthomeridion have previously been suggested to be homologs to the free cheeks of trilobites.
source: The ventral plates of Acanthomeridion have previously been suggested to be homologs to the free cheeks of trilobites, with the suture between these features and the remainder of the cephalon interpreted as a facial suture (Figure 1d) (e.g. Hou et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is a statement about previous interpretations supported by citation to Hou et al., 2017b.

claim: Morphological similarities are apparent between the ventral plates of Acanthomeridion and free cheeks in many trilobites.
source: Morphological similarities are apparent between the ventral plates and free cheeks in many trilobites (Figure 9a and b; Whittington et al., 1997) as well as the path of suture separating them from the rest of the cephalon.
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation supported by citation to Whittington et al., 1997 and reference to Figure 9.

claim: The ventral plates of Acanthomeridion are transversely broad, tapering posteriorly to a spine, in a position directly comparable to the genal spine of many trilobites.
source: The ventral plates of Acanthomeridion are here shown to be transversely broad, tapering posteriorly to a spine, in a position directly comparable to the genal spine of many trilobites (Figure 1d; Figure 9a, b).
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation based on specimens and figures.

claim: The ventral plate of Acanthomeridion is separated from the rest of the cephalon by a suture that passes near the compound eye.
source: Furthermore, the ventral plate is separated from the rest of the cephalon by a suture that passes near the compound eye.
evidence: This is a morphological observation based on specimens.

claim: The path of the suture in Acanthomeridion is similar to the facial suture of many trilobites especially those bearing opisthoparian facial sutures.
source: This path is similar to the facial suture (fused circumocular and marginal sutures) of many trilobites especially those bearing opisthoparian facial sutures, which separate the free cheeks from the cranidium passing through the visual surface (Figure 9a and b; Whittington et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation supported by citation to Whittington et al., 1997 and reference to Figure 9.

claim: The homology of eye notches and eye slits of petalopleurans, dorsal ecdysial sutures in trilobites and Acanthomeridion has been suggested previously.
source: The homology of eye notches (e.g. Luohuilinella and Zhiwenia [Figure 9e and f]), and eye slits (e.g. Phytophilaspis Ivantsov, 1999; Figure 9c and d) of petalopleurans, dorsal ecdysial sutures in trilobites and Acanthomeridion has been suggested previously (Du et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about previous interpretations supported by citation to Du et al., 2019.

claim: The evolution from eye notches to eye slits and finally to the loss of the eye slit has been inferred, calling into question the affinity between these structures and sutures.
source: However, the evolution from eye notches to eye slits and finally to the loss of the eye slit has been inferred, calling into question the affinity between these structures and sutures (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about previous interpretations supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: When the ventral plates of Acanthomeridion are considered homologous to the free cheeks of trilobites, Acanthomeridion is recovered sister to trilobites.
source: If ventral plates are considered homologous to free cheeks, Acanthomeridion is recovered sister to trilobites, however, dorsal ecdysial sutures are still recovered at many places within Artiopoda.
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: When the ventral plates of Acanthomeridion are considered homologous to free cheeks, dorsal ecdysial sutures are still recovered at many places within Artiopoda.
source: If ventral plates are considered homologous to free cheeks, Acanthomeridion is recovered sister to trilobites, however, dorsal ecdysial sutures are still recovered at many places within Artiopoda.
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: When ventral plates of Acanthomeridion are considered homologous to doublure or non-homologous, then Acanthomeridion is not recovered as sister to trilobites.
source: If ventral plates are considered homologous to doublure or non-homologous, then Acanthomeridion is not recovered as sister to trilobites, and thus the ventral plates represent a distinct feature to trilobite doublure/free cheeks.
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: All six Bayesian analyses produced the same broad relationships within Artiopoda, with the exception of the position of Acanthomeridion.
source: All six Bayesian analyses produced the same broad relationships within Artiopoda, with the exception of the position of Acanthomeridion (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analyses presented in the study.

claim: Petalopleurans were recovered sister to Nektaspida in the phylogenetic analyses.
source: Petalopleurans were recovered sister to Nektaspida, Australimicola sister to Conciliterga, and Vicissicaudata was not completely resolved.
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analyses presented in the study.

claim: Australimicola was recovered sister to Conciliterga in the phylogenetic analyses.
source: Petalopleurans were recovered sister to Nektaspida, Australimicola sister to Conciliterga, and Vicissicaudata was not completely resolved.
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analyses presented in the study.

claim: When the analysis was unconstrained, Olenellus and Eoredlichia formed a group sister to the other trilobites, or these two taxa were recovered in a polytomy with a clade containing the other trilobites.
source: Within Trilobita, when the analysis was unconstrained, Olenellus and Eoredlichia formed a group sister to the other trilobites, or these two taxa were recovered in a polytomy with a clade containing the other trilobites (Figure 10—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analyses presented in the study.

claim: When the group Anacherirurus, Cryptolithus, Eoredlichia, Olenoides, and Triarthrus was constrained (with the exclusion of Olenellus), then Olenellus was recovered as sister to all other trilobites.
source: When the group Anacherirurus, Cryptolithus, Eoredlichia, Olenoides, and Triarthrus was constrained (with the exclusion of Olenellus), then Olenellus was recovered as sister to all other trilobites (Figure 10—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analyses presented in the study.

claim: All consensus trees support multiple origins of cephalic sutures in Artiopoda.
source: All consensus trees support multiple origins of cephalic sutures in Artiopoda (Figure 10, Figure 10—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is a conclusion from phylogenetic analyses presented in the study.

claim: The exopodites of Acanthomeridion differ substantially from those known in other artiopodans.
source: The exopodites of Acanthomeridion also differ substantially from those known in other artiopodans.
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation based on specimens and literature.

claim: The stick-like nature of the exopodite of Acanthomeridion, the rows of lamellae combined with the apparent lack of segmentation, differ from the paddle-shaped exopodites thought to characterise the remainder of the group.
source: Specifically, the stick-like nature of the exopodite, the rows of lamellae combined with the apparent lack of segmentation, differ from the paddle-shaped exopodites thought to characterise the remainder of the group (e.g. Schmidt et al., 2022 and Figure 4 in Ortega-Hernández et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparative morphological observation supported by citations to Schmidt et al., 2022 and Ortega-Hernández et al., 2013.

claim: Multipodomerous uniramous deutocerebral antennae are known in nearly all other members of Artiopoda.
source: Multipodomerous uniramous deutocerebral antennae are known in nearly all other members of the clade (Zhang et al., 2007; Du et al., 2019; Zhai et al., 2019)
evidence: This is a statement about artiopodan morphology supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2007; Du et al., 2019; and Zhai et al., 2019.

claim: A conterminant hypostome was already known in numerous other artiopodans.
source: Similarly, a conterminant hypostome was already known in numerous other artiopodans (Zhang et al., 2004; Stein and Selden, 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about artiopodan morphology supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2004 and Stein and Selden, 2012.

claim: A conterminant type of hypostomal attachment is considered ancestral within Trilobita.
source: As this type of hypostomal attachment is considered ancestral within Trilobita (Fortey, 1990)
evidence: This is a statement about trilobite morphology supported by citation to Fortey, 1990.

claim: The presence of natant hypostomes in both trilobitomorphs and vicissicaudates demonstrates that a natant hypostome has most likely evolved repeatedly within Artiopoda.
source: If Acanthomeridion is instead an early diverging artiopodan, the presence of natant hypostomes in both trilobitomorphs and vicissicaudates (Fortey, 1990; Chen et al., 2019) demonstrates that a natant hypostome has most likely evolved repeatedly within Artiopoda.
